chapter_theme: Pattiragiriyar's lament continues on its one question, எக்காலம், 'when?': when will he pass beyond even eightfold yoga, set a ladder from the parted body to the ancient city, burn the sastras and the Vedas and find the one formula, know awareness by awareness and sleep without speech, and shoot his awareness as an arrow from the bow of the mind. The second half is a run of similes for the hidden becoming manifest: fire rising from the sea, the worm turned wasp in its nest, gold becoming ornaments, fire from bamboo, the sunstone that burns cotton only in the sun's presence, iron taking the form of fire.
structure_note: Couplets, each ending in the refrain எக்காலம். 151 to 166 ask about states (beyond yoga, pasu and pati, the end of the Veda, mukti); 169 to 175 each open with a போல் simile. Unit 168 is from a second edition and breaks the numbered run.

151.reading: Beyond the eight-limbed yoga, and beyond what lies beyond it, is the thing that is not reached; when will I reach it?
151.nuance: Ashtanga yoga is named only to be passed: the goal is placed past the practice twice over (அப்பாலுக்கு அப்பால்). The verse does not say what the unreached thing is.

152.reading: When body and life, which cling together without clinging, have parted, when will I set a ladder here to the ancient city that cannot be reached?
152.nuance: ஒட்டாமல் ஒட்டிநிற்கும் describes body and life as joined but not fused. பழம்பதி is the old abode and also the old Lord (பதி); the ladder is set 'here', in this life, which reads as a wish for release before death.

153.reading: Removing the bond, releasing the soul into the Lord, when will I stay in thought within love?
153.nuance: The three Siddhanta terms (பாசம், பசு, பதி) are used plainly, and the soul is sent into the Lord rather than made identical with him; 194 later collapses the three into one.

154.reading: Forgetting rules of conduct, attachment and ritual observance, when will I gain the state of speechless true knowledge?
154.nuance: ஆசாரம் and அனுட்டானம் are the orthodox terms for prescribed conduct and daily rites; they are to be forgotten, not reformed. The knowledge is பேசா, unspeaking.

155.reading: When will I know that the many thousand crores of cosmoses are your creation and nothing other than that?
155.nuance: அல்லாது வேறில்லை can mean that nothing exists besides his creation, or that the cosmoses are nothing but him; the first is the plainer reading.

156.reading: When will I recite, know and feel within me the letter called Hari, which stood as the first beginning?
156.nuance: அரி என்ற அட்சரம் is the crux. அரி is a name of Vishnu, which is odd in a Saiva poet unless, as with Sivavakkiyar's ராம verses, it is cipher; tradition also reads it as the primal letter அ, from which the others come, so that the letter and the First are one. The verse gives no help in choosing.

157.reading: Burning the sastras, making the four Vedas false, when will I see the one formula and cut off sorrow?
157.nuance: சூத்திரம் is the terse aphorism that holds a whole science, and also the string that works a puppet (as in 213); either way one hidden thing is set against the whole library, and sorrow ends with seeing it, not with reading.

158.reading: Knowing my awareness by awareness night and day, forgetting speech and what is spoken, when will I sleep?
158.nuance: தூங்குவது, sleeping, is the rest that follows when speech is forgotten, not slumber; 195 repeats the first phrase and sharpens it.

159.reading: When will I know the end of the Veda, which embraces all that moves and stands still as oil is in sesame?
159.nuance: வேத முடிவு is Vedanta in the literal sense, the Veda's end, and the thing it points to. The sesame image makes pervasion invisible and intimate: the oil is in every seed and nowhere to be seen.

160.reading: When will I know the one who stood as flesh, as life within the flesh, and as every world, himself?

161.reading: Since you stay in me and never leave me, when will I become one-pointed and never leave you?
161.nuance: The verse turns the Lord's constancy into a reproach to the poet's own inconstancy; ஒருப்படுதல் is to be resolved, of one mind.

162.reading: The limitless sky-thing that cannot be said to be 'this': when will I know it as what has been told, and tell it?
162.nuance: சொன்னதென்று நான் அறிந்து can mean knowing it to be what the teachers said, or knowing it as a thing that has been said at all. Either way the verse asks for the unsayable to be known and spoken, and leaves the contradiction standing.

163.reading: Making the mind a bow, the sky's spark its string and my awareness the arrow, when will I shoot?
163.nuance: The bow is the Mundaka Upanishad's (there Om is the bow and the self the arrow); here the mind is the bow and the target is not named. வான்பொறி, the spark of space, is taken by tradition as the inner light or the breath; the verse does not say.

164.reading: You who shot me so that I died, and wiped out my disgrace: when will I set you in the open and stand hidden?
164.nuance: எய்து continues the bow of 163, but the archer is now the Lord and the self the thing shot. வெளியில் வைத்து ஒளித்து நிற்பது asks for the Lord shown and the poet concealed, the ego's death made good; the syntax is compressed and the lines could be divided otherwise.

165.reading: Like a ferry-boat that is driven by thrusting bamboo poles, when will I know the picture that drives me?
165.nuance: சித்திரம் is a picture or a marvel, here the unseen mover of the boat; the body is the boat and the poles are the force from outside. 213 says the same with a puppet in the wind.

166.reading: Without shifting from the state I stand in, without anything attaching in thought, when will I join and know that the state I have gone to is mukti?

167.reading: Setting within the golden foot adorned with gold and silver, when will I shut it in the flashing space of light?
167.nuance: The gold and silver on the golden foot are read by tradition as the sun and moon breaths (pingala and ida) brought to the place where they meet, and ஒளிவெளி as the inner space of light; plainly it is the Lord's adorned feet placed within and the light closed in. The verb விட்டு அடைப்பது, letting go and shutting, is itself obscure.

168.reading: Water dwelling in water joining at the great foot: when will I say in a word how that is?
168.nuance: A unit from the second edition, without the question mark. Water in water is the stock figure for the soul merged in the Lord with no seam; the poet asks for a single word (ஒரு செப்பு) for what has no seam to describe.

169.reading: As the worm shut in the nest takes on the wasp's form, when will I, shut in the house, beg for grace?
169.nuance: In the stock image the worm becomes the wasp by dwelling on it; the poet asks to be shut in the same way and to want only grace. வீடு is a house (the body, or the wasp's cell) and also release, and both senses work.

170.reading: As the fire hidden in the sea rises up and comes, when will the Siva hidden in the body shine out?
170.nuance: The sea-fire is the vadavamukha of the Puranas, the fire that lies under the ocean until the end; Siva lies hidden in the body in the same way, present but unseen until he blazes.

171.reading: As the red light of dawn spreads over the whole cosmos, when will I stand merged in the compassionate holy feet?

172.reading: As many kinds of ornament come from gold, when will I be born in you and subside in you?
172.nuance: The ornament is gold in a shape and gold again when melted; birth and subsiding in the Lord keep the one substance. This is the Vedanta figure for the world's relation to Brahman.

173.reading: So that the sorrow of my being born in a birth lower than a dog's ends, when will I shine like fire-light in bamboo?
173.nuance: The fire latent in bamboo comes out by friction; the light is already in the poet's wretched birth. நாயிற் கடைப்பிறப்பு is the poet's self-abasement, a stance kept through the work.

174.reading: As the sunstone's light closes round cotton and burns it, when will I gain grace at the appearing of the noble one?
174.nuance: ஆரியன், the noble one, is the Lord or the guru. The sunstone burns only in the sun's presence, so the grace comes with the appearing (தோற்றம்), not with the stone's own effort.

175.reading: As iron with fire kindled in it leaves this form and takes that form, when will I find and know the sweet juice in the sugarcane?
175.nuance: Two images run together: iron that becomes fire is the soul taking the Lord's nature, and the juice hidden in the cane is the sweetness hidden in the body. How the second follows from the first is not spelled out.

links.note: Both place the goal past eightfold yoga: Tirumular says understanding of every kind lies beyond the eight siddhis that the yoga gives, and Pattiragiriyar asks for the thing beyond what is beyond the yoga. Neither rejects the practice; both refuse to stop at it.

A ladder to release in both: Tirumular's rungs are the thirty-six tattvas climbed upward; Pattiragiriyar's ladder is to be set here, once body and life have parted, to the ancient city that cannot be reached. The image is shared, the rungs are named only in Tirumular.

The first letter as the First Being: the Kural has the world begin from the Primal Lord as letters begin from அ; Pattiragiriyar wants to know within himself the letter that stood as the first beginning. The link holds on the reading of அரி as that primal letter, which is one of two.

Both end the library: Sivavakkiyar says the images, sastras, homa pit, four Vedas and bundled books all came to nothing once he knew the Lord; Pattiragiriyar asks when he will burn the sastras, make the Vedas false and see the one formula that cuts off sorrow.

163 makes the poet the archer, mind as bow and awareness as arrow; 164 turns the figure round, so that it is the Lord who shot the poet dead and wiped out his disgrace. The shooting the poet asked to do is done to him.
The body moved from outside, twice: a ferry driven by poles and a puppet turned by the wind. In 165 the poet wants to know the mover; in 213 he wants to see the body itself as the puppet it is.

The wasp's nest in both: Sivavakkiyar's worm in the fresh-clay cell becomes what it thinks of daily and flies; Pattiragiriyar asks to be shut in the same way and to beg for grace. Sivavakkiyar makes it a lesson in thinking, Pattiragiriyar a figure for confinement and asking.

Fire from bamboo: in Tirumular it is Nandi hidden in the body-temple who rises and removes the malas; in Pattiragiriyar it is the poet himself who hopes to shine out of a birth lower than a dog's. The latent fire is the Lord in one and the soul in the other.

The same image with the same point: the sunstone burns the cotton round it only in the sun's presence. Tirumular says the malas end when the sun appears; Pattiragiriyar asks for grace at the appearing (தோற்றம்) of the noble one. In both the burning waits on the presence, not on the stone.

source_issues: Unit 168 (id siddhar:meynjanap-pulambal:0155-148) is from a second edition: it is unnumbered in the main edition, lacks the refrain's question mark, and is interleaved into the numbered run between 167 and 169.
163 prints என தறிவை with a space inside the word (எனதறிவை).
